Revolters
rə-vōlt'ərz
n. pl. (those who turn away after having belonged; apostates within the covenant people)
French revolter, from Latin revolvere, to roll back. The Hebrew sarar and sur carry the same picture: to turn aside, to be stubborn, to go back from a place one had come to.

Biblical Definition

A revolter is not an outsider. The word belongs to the covenant people and names those who turned. Jeremiah's indictment is total: “They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters” (Jer 6:28). The metals are the point — the assayer looked for silver and found base metal all through. Hosea sees the same men at their worst, and with a terrible competence: “And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all” (Hos 5:2). Profound is the word for depth and skill; a people who once knew the law can apply real intelligence to evil. Later Hosea puts the revolt at the very top of the nation: “All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more: all their princes are revolters” (Hos 9:15). Isaiah opens his prophecy with the same grief in family terms: “I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me” (Isa 1:2). The tragedy of revolt is measured by the privilege it turns from.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a revolter as one who changes sides; one who abandons a party or a cause to which he had adhered, or who renounces his allegiance.

expand to see more

REVOLT, v.i. To fall off or turn from one to another.

2. To renounce allegiance and subjection to one's prince or state; to reject the authority of a sovereign.

REVOLTER, n. One who changes sides; one who abandons a party or a cause; an apostate.

They are all grievous revolters. Jer. vi.

Key Scripture

Jer 6:28 — "They are all grievous revolters, walking with slanders: they are brass and iron; they are all corrupters."

Hos 5:2 — "And the revolters are profound to make slaughter, though I have been a rebuker of them all."

Hos 9:15 — "All their wickedness is in Gilgal: for there I hated them: for the wickedness of their doings I will drive them out of mine house, I will love them no more: all their princes are revolters."

Isa 1:2 — "Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the LORD hath spoken, I have nourished and brought up children, and they have rebelled against me."

Modern Corruption

Turning from the faith one was raised in is now narrated as growth and honesty, though Scripture calls it revolt and grieves over it as a father grieves.

expand to see more

The public account of leaving the faith has been rewritten in our lifetime. What Jeremiah calls revolt is now told as a story of a man coming into his own — he examined what he had been given, found it wanting, and had the courage to walk. The telling is careful never to name a doctrine that was disproved, because usually none was; what changed was allegiance. Scripture is not impressed by the narrative and it is not fooled by the vocabulary. Hosea's revolters are profound, which is to say clever, articulate, capable of an impressive case; the prophet does not deny their ability, he denies their innocence. And Jeremiah's image of the assay is the answer to every claim that the departure simply revealed what was always there: the fire found brass and iron because brass and iron were what the ore contained. First John says the same thing without heat — they went out from us because they were not of us.

The second thing to name is where Hosea locates the revolt: all their princes are revolters. The rot did not begin with the common people; it came down from the men in office. That is the ordinary pattern in the histories, and it is a warning to every eldership. A congregation is rarely more faithful than its teachers for long. Against this the Lord sets the promise that makes recovery possible and that no revolter has ever exhausted: I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely. The doctrine of perseverance is not the claim that no professing man ever walks away — the prophets and the apostles say plainly that many do — but that no one whom the Father gave to the Son is finally lost. The right use of the word revolter is therefore self-examination before it is a label for someone else.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew sarar (H5637), to be stubborn, to turn away; sur (H5493), to turn aside; meshubah (H4878), backsliding, the noun of the same turning.

expand to see more

Hebrew sarar (H5637) — to turn away, to be stubborn or rebellious; the stubborn and rebellious son, and the revolting people; Deuteronomy 21:18, Jeremiah 6:28.

Hebrew sur (H5493) — to turn aside, to depart; used of princes who are revolters and companions of thieves; Hosea 9:15, Isaiah 1:23.

Hebrew meshubah (H4878) — backsliding, turning back; the word of the promise that God will heal it; Jeremiah 3:22, Hosea 14:4.

Hebrew marad (H4775) — to rebel, to revolt against a sovereign; the rebellion of Zedekiah against Babylon and of Israel against God; Ezekiel 17:15.

Greek apostasia (G646) — a standing away, apostasy; the falling away that precedes the day of Christ; 2 Thessalonians 2:3.

Usage

"“They are all grievous revolters” — the assay that found brass and iron."

"“The revolters are profound to make slaughter” — ability without allegiance."

"“All their princes are revolters” — the rot that came down from the men in office."
